When Rebrands Backfire: The Cracker Barrel Lesson See Page 5 Volume 6, Issue 128 Guest Editorial on SB79 Soroya Announces 2025-2026 Season See Page 10 See Page 4 ENCINO ENTERPRISE NEWS IN BRIEF ONEgeneration to Host Annual Touch a Truck Event Sept. 20 ONEgeneration will be hosting their family-friendly “Touch a Truck” event on Saturday, September 20, from 8 am to 12 pm at 17400 Victory Blvd. See, touch, and hear different types of vehicles! Climb in a dump truck, run the sirens on a police car and lift the hose of a fire truck. This interactive event has all of the vehicles with a function for essential work that kids see and wonder about. There will be a sensitivity hour with no sirens from 8 to 9 am. Plus, free children’s activities like bubbles, face painting and crafts. Tickets are $15 for adults and $10 for children with all proceeds benefitting ONEgeneration. Buy them at zeffy.com/en-US/ticketing/touch-a-truck-september-2025- onegeneration-family-event-in-encino. Encino Neighborhood Council to Host Harvest Moon Movie Night Fall is in the air and the Encino Neighborhood Council is celebrating the Harvest Moon with a movie night on Saturday, September 20, from 5:30 to 9 pm at Encino Park (16953 Ventura Blvd.) There will be face painting, free ice cream, free popcorn and a showing of the classic Speilberg film E.T. Bring your own blankets and low chairs. This free community event is also sponsored by Councilmember Raman and Assemblymember Gabriel. Red Barn Tarzana Closing; Will Become Metro Storage The Red Barn Feed & Saddlery at 18601 Oxnard Street, a fixture in the Tarzana community since the 1950’s, will close its doors November 1. Owned by Phil Carter from the 1980’s until his passing in 2023, Red Barn was a community hub where families could visit, pets could be pampered and animal lovers could connect. The new owners chose not to renew their lease and will close the store. Metro will re-purpose the property to support their facilities maintenance operations, including work on the G Line Bus Rapid Transit, and the future East San Fernando Valley Light Rail Transit, currently under construction on Van Nuys Blvd. A Compendious Source of Information September 18, 2025 Encino Community Zoom Let Locals Vent About Crime, Homelessness, and the Controversial SB79 Over 150 locals congregated on a Zoom meeting last night to discuss an array of pressing issues facing Encino. While increasing crime and security have been the major focus over the past few months, this meeting’s focus largely centered on the divisive bill, SB79. This bill permits multi-family, high- rise residential buildings to be built in single-family residential neighborhoods within a half mile of transit corridors despite any previously established zoning laws. (See related editorial on page 4.) The conversation, moderated by Encino Property Owners Association President Rob Glushon, got the most heated when arguing the potential detrimental effects if the bill is signed. Councilmember Nithya Raman, the featured guest speaker of the meeting, voted against the City Council resolution to veto the bill. (It is also worth noting that State Senator Henry Stern voted no, Mayor Bass voted no and Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel of Encino declined to vote.) In response to why she chose to vote as she did, Raman explained, “My vote was to engage with SB79. It puts us at a disadvantage point if we veto against it because we have a housing crisis and we need to build more affordable housing in Los Angeles. It’s important to engage with the bill’s goals.” As the majority of the Zoom attendees were residents of these potentially affected neighborhoods, the pushback was strong. After a testy back-and- forth, Glushon closed the topic by pronouncing, “You’re voting how you want and not representing Things got heated between EPOA Glushon and Raman when discussing SB79 on last night’s Zoom. us.” In the remaining time, Councilmember Raman and LAPD Senior Lead Officer Tim Walia gave various updates on crime and answered questions from participants, many of whom are still outraged at the current state of local matters including homelessness, traffic concerns and the increasing fires in Sepulveda Basin. General platitudes, calls to reach out to local government officials and requests for follow-ups were generously sprinkled throughout the conversation by Raman. Before disclosing the local crime stats, Walia confirmed that a large Hispanic crew responsible for multiple home burglaries throughout the Valley had been arrested on September 11 in the Westlake Sherwood area. Additionally, Walia warned that there is currently a known “distraction team” going around local shops and diverting customers’ attentions to then steal items from women’s purses. He urged everyone to not leave their purses in open sight, such as a shopping cart, and hold them close to the body instead. He disclosed that the current crime statistics for August were as follows: zero homicides, one rape, four burglaries (down from July, which had 30), six aggravated assaults, five motor vehicle thefts, 16 vehicle break- ins and 35 thefts. In regards to homelessness, Raman assured the attendees that her team is being aggressive in addressing the problem in Encino. With an established group solely dedicated to the homeless, their office knows the locations of various camps and knows the majority of the unhoused individuals by name who they are trying to get off the street in a sustainable manner. One local inquired about the potential problems that may arise from the Oak Tree Inn being converted into a shelter site. Raman went on to explain that the site is intended for 18 to 24-year-olds transitioning out of the foster system, many of whom are either in school or working. The site consists of 26 rooms, each individual has their own case manager working with them and the property is monitored by 24-hour security. The discussion of Oak Tree Inn sparked a heated discussion on the homelessness crisis in the area and the true cost of handling the issue. (continued to page 3)
Encino Enterprise, September 18, 2025, Page 6 HEALTH Legislation Passes Strengthening Penalties for Impersonationing First Responders During Emergencies The California State Legislature recently passed a pair of bipartisan bills to provide law enforcement with better tools to crack down on looting and impersonation of emergency personnel during wildfires and other emergencies. Not only is it grossly unethical, it impedes the health and safety of the community. Crimes like these endanger both the public and the first responders dedicated to protecting them. In the months following the devastating Southern California fires, impacted communities have been victimized further by widespread looting. Directly following the fires, law enforcement arrested dozens of individuals for looting and impersonation- related charges, including two individuals from Oregon charged with impersonating firefighters in the Palisades Fire evacuation zone. These actions pose significant risks to public safety and undermine evacuation efforts, leading to confusion and potentially deterring residents from following critical public safety guidance. Crimes like these endanger both the public and the first responders dedicated to protecting them. “Individuals who put our firefighters at risk and prey on communities when they are at their most vulnerable must be held accountable. Looters – particularly those who impersonate emergency personnel – create chaos and confusion, endanger residents and first responders, undermine public trust in evacuation orders, divert critical emergency resources, and victimize communities that already have suffered unimaginable harm. I am proud to join efforts with my Senate and Assembly colleagues to provide law enforcement with better tools to crack down on looting and impersonation, and I urge Governor Newsom to sign these important bills,” said Assemblymember Gabriel. AB 468 and SB 571 now head to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk, where they must be signed into law or vetoed by October 12. TIMING IS EVERYTHING. And the time is now at Fairwinds.
